text: rocket propulsion. Now we deal with the case where the mass of an object is changing. As a rocket lifts off, it burns fuel gases that cause a change to its velocity and hence its momentum. The acceleration is in the opposite direction of the velocity of the ejected fuel. Consider a fully fueled rocket ship in deep space that has a total mass M sub zero. Mass includes both the ship and the fuel. At some moment in time, the rocket has a velocity vector V and mass M. Mass includes the ship and only the remaining fuel. The rocket accelerates by burning the fuel it carries and ejecting the burned exhaust gases. If the burn rate of the fuel and the velocity at which the exhaust is ejected is constant, what is the change of velocity of the rocket as a result of burning all of its fuel? An organic chemistry tutor video is linked on the course webpage. Rockets accelerate by throwing mass backward. As you watch, focus on how the expelled fuel carries momentum in one direction while the rocket gains momentum in the opposite direction. The important point is that a rocket does not need air to push against. It accelerates by exchanging momentum with its own fuel. Physical analysis. Here's a more detailed description in physical terms. The rocket engines are continuously ejecting gases which have some momentum due to their mass and velocity. By conservation of momentum, the rocket's momentum changes by this same amount with the opposite sign. The rate of change of the momentum is constant because the rocket is burning fuel at a constant rate. From vector F equals D vector P divided by DT, there is a constant force on the rocket. As time goes on, the mass of the rocket continuously decreases because of the ejecting gases. Even though the force on the rocket is constant, the resulting acceleration is not. It is continuously increasing. Vector A equals vector F divided by M. The total change in the rocket's velocity will depend on the amount of fuel mass burned, and that dependence is not linear. The problem has the mass and velocity of the rocket changing along with the total mass of the ejected gases. Let's define our system to be the rocket plus fuel. Then this is a closed system since there are not external forces in deep space. As a result, momentum is conserved for this system. See the figure. And we can apply the conservation of momentum to answer the question. The total instantaneous mass of the rocket is M, i.e. the mass of the ship plus the amount of fuel at time T. We define the rocket's instantaneous velocity as vector V equals V i hat, where the velocity is measured relative to an inertial reference system, i.e. some star that is barely moving relative to the galactic center. Thus, the initial momentum of the system is vector P initial equals MV i hat. The rocket's engines are burning fuel at a constant rate and ejecting exhaust gases in the minus i hat direction. During an infinitesimal time DT, the engines eject a positive infinitesimal mass of gas, DMG, at velocity vector U equals minus U i hat. Note that the exhaust gas velocity is measured with respect to the moving rocket. The gas speed measured relative to the star is V minus U i hat. As a consequence of the ejection of the fuel gas, the rocket's mass decreases by DM sub G, and its velocity increases by DV i hat. We can write the new momentum vector P final after this change as vector P final equals vector P sub rocket plus vector P sub gas equals M minus DM sub G times V plus DV i hat plus DM sub G times V minus U i hat. Since all vectors are in the same direction, we drop the vector notation. Applying conservation of momentum, we have P initial equals P final. MV equals M minus DM sub G times V plus DV plus DM sub G times V minus U. MV equals MV plus M DV minus DM sub G V minus DM sub G DV minus DM sub G U. M DV equals DM sub G DV plus DM sub G U. Now DM sub G and DV are each very small infinitesimal even, thus their product very, very small and we neglect this term. This is similar to adding a nanometer to a kilometer, it's still roughly a kilometer. We obtain M DV equals DM sub G U. Since DM sub G represents an increase in the mass of ejected gases, it must also represent a decrease in the mass of the rocket. DM sub G equals negative DM. Then we have M DV equals negative DM U. DV equals negative U times DM over M. Integrating from the initial mass M sub O to the final mass M gives us integral sub V sub I to the power of V DV equals minus U integral sub M sub O to the power of M DM over M. V minus V sub I equals U natural log of M sub O over M. This result is called the rocket equation and is typically given as a difference equation. Change in V equals U natural log of M sub O over M. It was originally derived by the Russian rocket scientist Constantine Sielkovsky in 1897. It gives us the change in velocity that the rocket obtains from burning a mass of fuel that decreases the total rocket mass from M sub O to M. Problem solving strategy, rocket propulsion. In rocket problems, the most common questions are finding the change in V due to burning some amount of fuel for some amount of time or to determine the acceleration A that results from burning fuel. First, to determine the change in V, use the rocket equation directly. Second, to determine the acceleration, determine the force by using the impulse momentum theorem where the rocket equation determines the change in velocity. Checkpoint. Pause and check your understanding. For a rocket, why can the force be constant while the acceleration changes with time? Example problem. Thrust on a spacecraft. The problem. A spacecraft moves in deep space along a straight path. Its thrusters eject fuel at a constant rate of 200 kilograms per second with an exhaust speed relative to the rocket of 250 meters per second. The initial mass of the spacecraft, including fuel, is 2.0 times 10 to the fourth kilograms and the thrusters fire for 30 seconds. A, what is the thrust on the spacecraft? B, what is the spacecraft's acceleration as a function of time while the thrusters fire? C, what are the accelerations at T equals 0, 15, 30 and 35 seconds? The worked solution. The model. We define the system as the spacecraft. The thrust arises from conservation of momentum. Fuel is expelled backward, giving the spacecraft forward momentum. Because fuel is ejected at a constant rate and constant exhaust speed, the thrust force is constant. However, the spacecraft's mass decreases with time as fuel is burned. Therefore, although the force is constant, the acceleration is not constant. We define the forward direction as positive. The math. The thrust equals the rate at which momentum is carried away by the exhaust. Since the exhaust speed is constant, F equals V sub exhaust times M dot equals 250 meters per second times 200 kilograms per second equals 5.0 times 10 to the fourth Newton's. While the engine's fire, the spacecraft's mass decreases linearly. M of T equals M minus M dot times T. From Newton's second law, the acceleration is A of T equals F divided by M of T, which equals F divided by the quantity M minus M dot times T, which equals 5.0 times 10 to the fourth Newton's divided by the quantity 2.0 times 10 to the fourth kilograms minus 200 kilograms per second times T. Now we evaluate at the time T equals 0, 15, 30 and 35 seconds. A of 0 equals 5.0 times 10 to the fourth Newton's divided by 2.0 times 10 to the fourth kilograms, which equals 2.5 meters per second squared. A of 15 seconds equals 5.0 times 10 to the fourth Newton's divided by 1.7 times 10 to the fourth kilograms, which equals 2.9 meters per second squared. A of 30 seconds equals 5.0 times 10 to the fourth Newton's divided by 1.4 times 10 to the fourth kilograms, which equals 3.6 meters per second squared. After T equals 30 seconds, the thrusters are off and F equals 0, so A of 35 seconds equals 0. The conclusion, the thrust on the spacecraft is F equals 5.0 times 10 to the four Newton's. While the engines fire, the acceleration is given by A of T equals 5.0 times 10 to the four Newton's divided by the quantity 2.0 times 10 to the four kilograms minus 2.0 times 10 to the two kilograms per second times T. The acceleration increases from 2.5 meters per second squared at launch to 3.6 meters per second squared at 30 seconds because the mass decreases as fuel is burned. Once the thrusters stop, the acceleration drops to 0 and the spacecraft continues at constant velocity. Rocket in a gravitational field. Let's analyze the rocket's velocity change during the launch phase from the surface of the Earth. For simplicity, we consider cases where the acceleration due to gravity is approximately a constant G. The analysis is similar except there is an external force vector F equals negative MGJ hat acting on our system. This force applies in impulse D vector J equals vector F DT, which equals negative MGDTJ hat and is equal to the change of momentum. This gives us D vector J equals D vector P, negative MGDTJ hat equals vector P final minus vector P initial, which equals the quantity M minus DM sub G times V plus DV plus DM sub G times V minus U minus MV all in the J hat direction. Therefore, negative MGDT equals MDV minus DM sub G U, where we neglect the term DM sub G DV and drop the vector notation. Replacing DM sub G with negative DM gives negative MGDT equals MDV plus DM U and MDV equals negative DM U minus MGDT. Dividing through by M to solve for V gives us DV equals negative U times the natural logarithm of M sub O over M minus G delta T. Unsurprisingly, the rocket's velocity is affected by the constant acceleration of gravity. The burn time of the fuel is represented by delta T. In the absence of gravity, it makes no difference how much time it takes to burn the entire mass of fuel because delta V is independent of delta T. The negative G delta T term tells us that the longer the burn time is, the smaller the rocket's change of velocity will be. This is why for a rocket launch, it is essential to burn the fuel as quickly as possible to get a large delta V.
